title: Designing Object-Oriented Programs
lede: Use SOLID and GRASP as questions about real code: who owns the data, who makes decisions, which changes stay local, and what callers can expect from a replacement.

sections.title: Responsibility and information experts
concepts: One reason to change

Start with one question: who is responsible for what? A responsibility is something a class knows or does.

The single responsibility principle (the S in SOLID) says a class should have one responsibility. Robert C. Martin, who named it, calls this one reason to change.

Test it with likely change requests: “Prices now include tax.” “Add the shop’s address to the receipt.” “Save as JSON too.” If all three land in one class, an edit for one job can break the other two. Today’s revision ReportJob was like this.

One responsibility is not one method. An Order with add, total and lineCount is one job: same data, same rules.

Common mistake: the over-correction

Splitting every method into its own class (OrderAdder, OrderTotaller, OrderCounter) scatters one idea over many files. Group code by reason to change, not by size.
Put a calculation beside its data

Information Expert: give a job to the class that already has the information for it. It is the first pattern of GRASP (General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns, from Craig Larman’s Applying UML and Patterns).

  • A line has the price and quantity, so it gets Line.subtotal().
  • An order has the lines, so Order.total() asks each line.

The slogan is tell, don’t ask. Tell an object to do the job. Do not take its data and do the job yourself. A caller that writes line.getCents() * line.getQuantity() now owns a copy of the subtotal rule.

Common mistake: a getter for every field

A getter and setter for every private field is not encapsulation. Callers still take the data and write the rules. Before adding a getter, ask whether the object should do the job instead.
Finding classes: nouns, verbs, CRC cards

In a problem description, nouns suggest classes or their data. Verbs suggest methods. The first diagram below tries this.

Words in the descriptionOften becomesExample
“a customer places an order”a classOrder
“each line has a price and a quantity”fields of another classLine.cents, Line.quantity
“the shop works out the total”a method, on the class that has the dataOrder.total()
“students get a discount, staff get another”something that varies: an interface or a functionPriceRule

It is a start, not an algorithm. A price is just an int. A receipt formatter is useful but never appears as a noun. GRASP calls an invented helper like that a Pure Fabrication.

CRC cards (Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators; Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham, 1989) test a design on index cards before any code. One card per class: name on top, responsibilities on the left, collaborators on the right. A full card means too many jobs. Data on no card has no owner.

OrderCollaborators
knows its lines
adds a line
works out the total		Line

If the only honest name is OrderManager or ReceiptAndFileHelper, the class probably has more than one job.
Creator: who makes the object?

GRASP’s Creator: class B should create A objects if B contains A, closely uses A, or has the data to set A up.

An order contains its lines, so order.addLine(300, 2) creates the Line itself. Callers never see Line, so you can change how lines are stored without touching them. Compare the first example below (main builds each line) with the extra The order creates its own lines. Both print 750.

Guarding data in each language:

IdeaJavaPython
hide a fieldprivate int cents; — the compiler refuses outside accessself._cents — a convention only; nothing stops access
a field that never changesprivate final int cents;no keyword; just never assign it again
read-only accessa getter and no settera @property with no setter
behaviour that needs no objecta static method inside some classa plain function in the module (often clearer)
A quick self-check

Finish the sentence “this class can do this because it has ___”. If the blank is another class’s field, the method probably belongs there.

customer.why: A person outside the program. Nothing here stores customer data, so no class is needed yet. Not every noun becomes a class.

order.why: An order is a thing with its own data (its lines) and its own jobs: a class, Order.

lines.why: A plural noun usually means several objects of one class: Line.

price.why: A value a line holds: the field cents.

quantity.why: A value a line holds: the field quantity.

add.why: Something the program does to an order: the method add.

subtotal.why: A noun, but it is worked out from price × quantity, so it becomes the method subtotal(). A stored copy would have to be kept up to date.

print.why: A verb: something the program does. Section 1.1 asks who should do it.

total.why: Also worked out, from the lines, so it becomes the method total(), not a stored number.

duties.label: add a line to the order

why.Order: Right: the order owns the list, so only the order should change it.
why.Line: A line does not know which order it belongs to, or that order's list.
why.main: main would have to reach into the order's private list. Let the order look after its own list.

why.Line: Right: price × quantity needs exactly the two numbers a line has.
why.Order: Then Order must read every line's price and quantity. It becomes coupled to Line's fields, and the rule sits away from its data.
why.main: main does not have the price or the quantity; it would have to dig them out of each line.

why.Order: Right: the order knows all of its lines, and asks each one for its subtotal.
why.Line: One line cannot see the other lines of its order.

why.main: Right: showing the result has a different reason to change (wording, layout) from calculating it. So it stays outside Order.
why.Order: Possible, but then Order changes whenever the output wording or layout changes: a second reason to change (1.1).
why.Line: A line knows nothing about the whole order's total.

steps.say: main creates an empty Order. The order owns its list of lines.
A new Line is built with its unit price and quantity. Those two numbers now live inside the line.
main sends add to the order, and the order puts the line in its own list.
A second line: 150 cents, quantity 1.
The order now holds two lines.
main asks the order for its total. main does not need to know how it is worked out.
The order knows its lines, so adding up is its job. It starts with sum = 0.
The order does not read cents or quantity itself. It asks line 1, which has those numbers.
Line 1 works out 300 × 2 and returns 600. The order adds it: sum is 600.
Next time round the loop, the order asks line 2.
Line 2 returns 150 × 1 = 150, so sum is 750.
There are no more lines. total() returns 750 to main.
main prints the number. Each calculation stayed with the object that had its data.
The program makes an Order holding two amounts. Calculating with them is the order's job.
The first print asks the order for its total.
The number is printed.
Now the receipt. Wording has a different reason to change, so it lives in its own function.
format_receipt does not add the amounts again. It asks the order, so there is only one adding-up rule.
The order answers 750, using the same total() as before.
The function puts the number into words and returns the text.
Change the wording: only format_receipt changes. Change the pricing: only Order changes.

media.alt: A very large red Swiss Army knife on a display stand with dozens of tools folded out at once: blades, scissors, pliers, saws, screwdrivers and more
media.lead: One body, many reasons to send it for repair.
media.caption: This Swiss Army knife packs blades, scissors, pliers, saws and dozens more tools into one body. Handy in a pocket; awkward as a design. If the scissors jam, the whole knife goes in for repair, saw and blades included. A class that calculates prices, words the receipt and saves the file is the same: a change for any one of those reasons opens code that serves the others. Where it breaks: one coherent job can still need several methods, just as a blade needs a hinge and a lock. Split by reason to change, not by counting methods.

media.alt: An old black taxi meter mounted beside a cab door, with counters labelled miles, recording mile and extras, and a maker's plate underneath
media.lead: The meter has the numbers, so the meter does the sum.
media.caption: This old London taxi meter counts the distance and the extras as the trip goes on, so it is the meter that shows the fare. Nobody asks the passenger to read its gears and work the fare out. That is Information Expert: give a job to the object that already has the information. A Line has its price and quantity, so it computes its subtotal; an Order has its lines, so it adds them up.

media.title: Good Code
media.alt: xkcd flowchart titled How to write good code. Start project, then: do things right or do them fast? Fast: code fast, does it work yet? No, loop; almost, but it has become a mass of kludges and spaghetti code. Right: code well, are you done yet? No, loop; no, and the requirements have changed. Both paths lead to: throw it all out and start over. Good code is reached only from a disconnected question mark.
media.caption: Requirements will change. Good design does not stop that; it keeps each change small and in one place, so you do not have to throw it all out.

notes: The leading underscore says “internal: use the methods”. Python does not enforce it; it is a promise between programmers.
The caller tells the account to withdraw. The rule “never go below zero” lives here, once.

Only 70 is left, so the account refuses and the balance stays the same. If callers checked the balance themselves, every caller would repeat that check.

sections.title: Extension and dependency inversion
concepts: Name the variation you need

The open–closed principle (the O in SOLID) comes from Bertrand Meyer’s 1988 book Object-Oriented Software Construction. Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification. You add a case with new code, not by editing code that works.

With a PriceRule, a half-price offer is a new HalfPrice class, and Basket is not opened. A basket that decides for itself grows one if per offer:

int price(int cents) {
    if (kind.equals("student")) return cents * 80 / 100;
    if (kind.equals("half")) return cents / 2;   // edit Basket again
    return cents;
}
Common mistake: an interface for everything

Add an interface only when real alternatives exist. One made “in case”, with a single implementation, is extra code to read. When the second case arrives, extracting it takes minutes.
Pass collaborators in

The dependency inversion principle (the D in SOLID): high-level policy should depend on an abstraction, not on a low-level detail. Here “price a basket” is the policy, “which discount” is the detail, and PriceRule is the abstraction. Basket and every rule depend on it. Neither knows the other.

Dependency injection means passing the collaborator in, often through the constructor: new Basket(new StudentPrice()). main chooses the rule. Basket just uses it.

In Python, functions are values. For one small operation, pass a function instead of building classes.

Python trap: / is not Java’s /

In Java, cents * 80 / 100 with ints gives 800. In Python, 1000 * 80 / 100 gives 800.0, a float. Use // for cents, as the Python example does.
Know what you depend on

A class that creates its own collaborators hides them. A Greeter that reads the system clock cannot test its “Good afternoon” branch in the morning. Give it a clock, and a test can pass a fake that always says 9 or 15. See the extra A fake clock makes the test repeatable.

Inject anything slow, random or outside the program: files, the network, the time, random numbers.

IdeaJavaPython
the contractinterface PriceRule { int apply(int c); }any callable; an ABC or Protocol for bigger contracts
a one-off small policya lambda for a one-method interface: c -> c / 2a function, or lambda c: c // 2
supply itnew Basket(new StudentPrice())Basket(student_price)
pass the wrong kind of thingcompile erroran error only when it is called
One tiny package, 2.5 hours

On 22 March 2016 a developer unpublished his kik package and 272 others from npm, the JavaScript package registry. One was left-pad, a tiny function many projects used without knowing, through other packages. npm saw hundreds of build failures per minute, and the disruption lasted 2.5 hours. Source: npm blog, “kik, left-pad, and npm”. Know exactly what you depend on.
Polymorphism instead of a growing if-chain

GRASP Polymorphism: when behaviour varies by type, give each type its own method instead of testing the type with if. Then rule.apply(cents) runs the right version. Week 8 showed how. This week is about when.

SituationPrefer
two or three fixed cases that rarely changea plain if/elif or switch
new cases keep arriving, each with its own rulesan interface and one class per case
one small operation variesPython: pass a function. Java: a one-method interface (or a lambda)
the cases differ only by a numberone class with a parameter, e.g. Discount(20)

All problems in computer science can be solved by another level of indirection… except for the problem of too many layers of indirection.

David Wheeler, as quoted by Butler Lampson; the second half is often given as Wheeler’s own conclusion

Every interface is one more place a reader must look. Add one only when it keeps a change small and local.

examples.code:
def student_price(cents): return cents*80//100

media.alt: A screwdriver with a blue and black handle and a long shaft, next to a holder of ten interchangeable Torx bits labelled T7 to T40
media.lead: Swap the bit, keep the handle.
media.caption: The handle never changes; every bit fits the same hexagonal socket. A new kind of screw needs a new bit, not a new screwdriver. That is what PriceRule gives Basket: a new pricing policy is a new class that fits the same socket, and Basket's code stays untouched. Where it breaks: a socket is only worth making when there really are several bits. A screwdriver for one kind of screw can have a fixed tip, and a class with one behaviour needs no interface yet.

media.alt: The front of a camera body with no lens attached: a metal bayonet ring with screws, a red alignment dot and a row of gold electrical contacts around the opening
media.lead: The camera depends on the mount, not on one lens.
media.caption: The ring on this camera body is a standard lens mount, with contacts the camera uses to talk to the lens. The body has no lens built in: you attach one, and any lens made for this mount will work. Dependency inversion is the same arrangement. Basket depends on the PriceRule contract, and the caller attaches a particular rule through the constructor, so the choice is visible where the objects are put together instead of hidden inside the basket.

sections.title: Substitution and focused interfaces
concepts: The signature is only part of the contract

The Liskov substitution principle (the L in SOLID): a replacement must keep the promises its callers rely on. Barbara Liskov set out the idea in a 1987 keynote, Data Abstraction and Hierarchy. In 1994 she and Jeannette Wing made it precise.

The compiler checks signatures, not behaviour. A List whose add inserted at the front would compile, and break every caller that expects append order.

A replacement may……but must not
accept more inputs than the originalrefuse inputs the original accepted
promise more (faster, more precise)promise less (wrong order, values lost)
store its data differentlyadd surprising side effects: printing, deleting, sending

Even Java’s List documentation marks add as an optional operation. Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list, so this compiles and then throws:

List<String> names = Arrays.asList("An", "Binh");
names.add("Mai");   // UnsupportedOperationException
Give callers only what they use

The interface segregation principle (the I in SOLID): callers should not depend on operations they never use. A notifier needs send, not a whole service that also stores data and deletes users.

A narrow interface:

  • shields callers from changes to other operations
  • is easy to implement: one method
  • lets a test pass a recorder that keeps messages instead of sending them

Python often has no interface at all. notify accepts any object with a send method. This is duck typing (“if it quacks like a duck…”). The fewer methods you call on a parameter, the more objects fit.
The classic trap: is a square a rectangle?

In maths every square is a rectangle, so class Square extends Rectangle looks right. In the extra A square that breaks a rectangle’s promise, a method sets width 5 and height 4 and expects an area of 20. A rectangle gives 20. A square keeps its sides equal and gives 16.

It compiles and runs, but it breaks the rectangle’s promise: “setting the height does not change the width”.

Common mistake: trusting the English “is a”

“A square is a rectangle” and “a penguin is a bird” both make broken subclasses if Rectangle has independent setters or Bird has fly(). Ask: can it do everything the parent promises, in every situation? If not, use a shared interface (Shape with area()) or composition.

One way out

Make shapes unchangeable: new Rectangle(5, 4) and new Square(4), with no setters. Then there is no promise to break, and both can implement Shape.
Contracts in Java and in Python

Both languages can state a contract. They check it at different moments. Only tests check behaviour.

IdeaJavaPython
declare a contractinterface Channel { String send(String m); }nothing (duck typing), or a class with ABC and @abstractmethod, or typing.Protocol
a method is missingcompile errorplain class: AttributeError when called.
ABC: TypeError when the object is created
mark an override@Override, checked by the compiler@typing.override (Python 3.12+), checked only by tools such as type checkers
the behaviour is wrongteststests
Common mistake: leaving out @Override

Misspell an override (tostring() instead of toString()) and Java quietly adds a new method. With @Override, the compiler reports the mistake at once. Use it every time.

sections.try: Write a send implementation that silently drops messages. Why does a matching method signature not prove it is a suitable replacement?

visuals.title: Swap the implementation: does it keep the promise?
visuals.intro: Each replacement is accepted: the Java ones compile and the Python ones run without an error. But does the caller still get what it relies on? Pick one, predict, then reveal the real output.

cases.label: Java: a List for fill()
cases.relies: fill(xs) relies on the List promise that add puts each element at the end. After fill, the list must hold 2 then 3, equal to the ArrayList a.

variants.label: LinkedList
variants.why: A different data structure inside (linked nodes, not an array), but the same promise: add appends.

variants.label: Vector
variants.why: An older List class from Java 1.0. It also keeps the promise, so the caller cannot tell the difference.

variants.label: FrontList (home-made)
variants.why: FrontList is a List, so the compiler accepts it. But its add puts each element at the front, so b ends up [3, 2]. Same signature, different behaviour.

cases.label: Python: a channel for notify()
cases.relies: The test relies on a recorder that keeps every message exactly as sent, so that recorder.messages shows what notify sent.

variants.label: Recorder (append)
variants.why: The example below: it records the message and returns "recorded".

variants.label: Recorder (+=)
variants.why: Different code inside, same behaviour: += [message] also adds to the end of the list.

variants.label: Recorder that drops
variants.why: It has send and says "recorded", but it never keeps the message. A test using it would pass while checking nothing.

variants.label: Recorder that shouts
variants.why: It changes the message before keeping it, so the test sees something notify never sent.

visuals.title: Callers that depend only on the promise
visuals.intro: fill and notify know only what their parameter promises to do. Step through: neither ever asks which class it was given.

steps.say: a is an ArrayList, declared with the interface type List<Integer>.
b is a LinkedList: different storage, same List type.
fill receives a as xs. It only knows that xs is some List.
Two add calls. The List promise: each element goes on the end.
The same method, now with the LinkedList. No if, no check of the class.
LinkedList keeps the same promise, so b also holds 2 then 3.
List equality compares the elements in order, whatever the class, so this is true.
The first element is 2, because add appended. A caller may rely on that.
A Recorder starts with an empty list of messages.
notify gets the recorder as channel. It needs exactly one capability from it: send.
It calls channel.send(message). A Screen, or anything else with a suitable send, would also work.
The recorder keeps the message instead of showing it, so a test can look at it afterwards.
send returns its answer.
notify passes it straight back, and it is printed.
The test checks the interaction itself: exactly one message, Ready, was sent. No real screen or email was involved.

visuals.title: One big interface or a narrow one?
visuals.intro: notify only calls send. In the first version its parameter is a large MessageService that also manages user accounts. In the second it is a one-method Channel. Make the two changes in order and watch which classes are dragged in.

changes.label: 1. Add a test recorder
changes.ask: Testing notify needs a recorder that keeps the messages instead of showing them.

changes.label: 2. Accounts gain resetPassword
changes.ask: After change 1, account management needs a new operation, resetPassword. notify does not use it.

fat:rec.note: The recorder must implement every MessageService method, so it gets two dummy methods for account jobs it will never do.

fat:reset.note: An account change forces edits to Screen and Recorder, two classes that only send messages. Their code was opened for a reason that has nothing to do with them.

narrow:rec.note: The recorder implements the one method notify needs. No dummy methods.

narrow:reset.note: Only Accounts changes. (Whatever class manages accounts would implement it; it is not part of this program.) Screen and Recorder are untouched.

visuals.summary: A client should not depend on operations it does not use. With the narrow interface, an account change never reaches the classes that only send messages.

media.lead: It fits the same bolts. It is not the same tyre.
media.caption: This temporary spare bolts on exactly like a normal wheel: the "signature" matches. But the sidewall says TEMPORARY USE ONLY, and the sticker and the sidewall limit the car to 80 km/h (50 mph). A driver who expects normal behaviour is in for a surprise. Liskov substitution asks for more than a matching shape: a replacement must keep the promises its callers rely on, such as a List keeping elements in the order they were added.

media.alt: Two car keys and a remote fob on a ring: a black-headed main key, and a separate green-headed valet key lying in front
media.lead: Hand over only what the job needs.
media.caption: Some cars came with a separate valet key (green, in front) as well as the main key, so that a parking attendant can drive the car without getting everything the owner's key can do. A narrow interface does the same for code: notify receives something that can send, not a whole service that can also delete users. Less to depend on means less that can break it, and a test can hand over a simple recorder instead.

media.alt: Artist's drawing of the Mars Climate Orbiter: a gold-wrapped box with a long solar panel and a dish antenna, above the orange surface of Mars
media.text: In September 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter. The interface specification said a ground program must report thruster impulse in newton-seconds; it reported pound-force seconds instead, so the navigation software underestimated the thrusters' effect by a factor of 4.45 and steered the spacecraft too close to Mars. Both programs passed numbers that "fitted". The broken part was the promise about what the numbers meant. Sources:
sources: NASA Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I report (1999)

media.alt: The Great Dome of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology behind a row of columns, seen along a cleared path between snowy lawns
media.text: The Liskov substitution principle is named after Barbara Liskov, a computer scientist at MIT. In 2009 she received the ACM A.M. Turing Award for her work on data abstraction, which MIT News described as a way to make software easier to construct, modify and maintain. She also designed the programming language CLU. Sources:

extras.title: A square that breaks a rectangle's promise
notes: Written for rectangles. It relies on a promise: setting the height leaves the width alone.
For a 5 by 4 rectangle the caller expects 20.
This compiles: a Square is a Rectangle as far as Java’s types go.
void setHeight(int h) { width = h; height = h; }
To stay square it changes the width too. Height 4 makes it 4 by 4, so the area is 16, not 20.
True in maths, false as a substitute: a square cannot keep a rectangle’s promise about independent sides.

sections.title: Cohesion, coupling and practical restraint
concepts: Coordinate without owning the rules

A GRASP Controller is the first object beyond the user interface to receive a request from outside, such as a button press or a line of input. It passes the work to the right model objects. It does not own the rules.

Counter.borrow() turns a request into stock.take() and a reply. The availability rule stays in Stock, the expert.

  • Cohesion: how closely the parts of one class belong together. Aim high.
  • Coupling: how much one class depends on another’s details. Aim low.
Common mistake: the class that does everything

A controller that checks stock, computes fines, formats messages and writes the log is the Swiss Army knife again. If a controller method grows past a few lines, hand work to an expert.
One home for each rule

DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) comes from Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas’s The Pragmatic Programmer (1999): “Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system.” It is about knowledge, not text that looks alike.

YAGNI (“You Aren’t Gonna Need It”) comes from Extreme Programming. Martin Fowler traces it to Kent Beck answering a list of features “the system would soon need” with “you aren’t going to need it”. Build what you need now.

Use GRASP names (Creator, Polymorphism, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, Protected Variations) to explain a design, not to add layers to a small program.

Common mistake: merging things that only look the same

The pass mark is 50 and the late-penalty cap is also 50. One shared constant couples two unrelated rules, so changing one silently changes the other. Ask: “if this one changed, must that one change too?” Only a yes means it is the same knowledge.

“There are two ways of constructing a software design: One way is to make it so simple that there are obviously no deficiencies and the other way is to make it so complicated that there are no obvious deficiencies. The first method is far more difficult.”

C. A. R. Hoare, The Emperor’s Old Clothes, 1980 ACM Turing Award Lecture, CACM 24(2), 1981 Portrait: Rama, 2011 · CC BY-SA 2.0 fr
Coupling you can see: long chains of dots

To spot tight coupling, count the dots:

String city = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity();   // knows three classes
String city = order.deliveryCity();                          // knows one

The first line depends on the insides of orders, customers and addresses. If customers get several addresses, it breaks. The second line asks only the order.

This is the Law of Demeter: “talk only to your immediate friends”. Ian Holland proposed it in 1987, on the Demeter project at Northeastern University.

A guideline, not a law

Chains on values are fine: name.strip().lower() or sb.append(a).append(b). The smell is walking through several different objects to reach some data.
Refactoring: change the design, keep the behaviour

Martin Fowler’s book Refactoring defines it as “a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior.”

Work in small steps: have a test or a known output, make one change, run it, repeat. The last diagram below shows four such steps. The extra Refactor, then prove nothing changed prints True when the old and new versions agree.

RefactoringUse it whenThis week
Renamea name no longer says what the thing doesdoIt → borrow
Extract method / functiona block of code has a job you can namepasses(mark)
Move methoda method uses another class’s data more than its ownsubtotal moves into Line
Replace conditional with polymorphisman if-chain on a type keeps growingPriceRule classes
Delete dead codenothing calls it any moreold code paths, unused flags
Common mistake: refactoring and adding a feature at once

If the output then changes, you cannot tell which edit caused it. Refactor until the output is identical, then add the feature.

Code that was “not meant to be used”

On 1 August 2012, in the first 45 minutes of trading, Knight Capital’s router sent more than 4 million orders while trying to fill 212 customer orders, and the firm lost more than $460 million. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found an old function left defective when code was moved in 2005: “although this function was not meant to be used, Knight left it in the router”. In late July 2012 Knight incorrectly deployed new code in the same router. Source: SEC press release 2013-222. If nothing needs some code, delete it.

“Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability.”

E. W. Dijkstra, EWD 498, How do we tell truths that might hurt?, 1975 Portrait: Hamilton Richards, 2002 · CC BY-SA 3.0

visuals.intro: Five jobs are in the wrong place. A red arrow means a class does a job that needs another class's data or role. The grey arrows are the two calls the program really needs. Select a job, then press Move here on the class that should own it.

classes.label: main (UI)
classes.calledBy: Nothing calls main: the program starts here. It calls counter.borrow().

classes.calledBy: Called by Counter (take()). It calls nobody.

take one copy (count − 1)

visuals.title: A controller coordinates, the expert decides
visuals.intro: Step through three borrow requests. Watch count inside the Stock. The Counter never touches it: it only asks.

steps.say: A Stock with 2 copies. count is private: only Stock can change it.
The Counter is given the Stock it will work with (it does not create its own).
First request: main asks the controller.
The Counter asks the expert. Stock checks count == 0 (false), lowers count to 1 and will return true.
The Counter turns true into the reply "Borrowed".
main prints the reply.
Second request.
One copy is still there, so count goes from 1 to 0 and take returns true.
Borrowed again.
Third request.
Now count == 0 is true: take returns false and leaves count alone. It cannot go negative.
The Counter turns false into "Unavailable". It made no decision about stock itself.
The availability rule lives in one place, Stock. The Counter just coordinates.
Three marks. The pass rule is written once, in passes.

steps.at: return sum(passes(mark) for mark in marks)
steps.say: count_passes does not know the pass mark. It asks passes about each mark.
49 >= 50 is False.
50 >= 50 is True: exactly 50 passes.
85 passes too.
sum counts each True as 1, so the count is 2.

steps.at: return ["P" if passes(mark) else "F" for mark in marks]
steps.say: labels asks the very same function, so it cannot disagree with the count.
Same three answers, turned into "F", "P", "P".

visuals.title: Refactor step by step: from one long main to Counter and Stock
visuals.intro: Refactoring changes the design, not what the program does. Step through four small moves that turn a copy-and-paste main into the controller example below. Each step checks that the real output stayed the same.

steps.title: Start: everything in main
steps.why: It works, but the stock rule is pasted three times. main does everything: holds the count, applies the rule, chooses the reply and prints it.

steps.title: Give the data a home: a Stock class
steps.why: The count now belongs to an object. But main still reads and changes stock.count directly, so it is coupled to Stock's field and still holds the rule.

steps.title: Move the rule beside its data: take()
steps.why: Stock owns count, so Stock gets the rule. The field becomes private, the rule exists once, and nobody outside can make the count negative.

steps.title: Give the request a coordinator: Counter
steps.why: Turning a request into a model call and a reply is now the Counter's job. main only starts things and prints. This is the example below.

steps.title: Stop here
steps.why: Tempting next steps: a BorrowPolicy interface, a factory, a configuration file. With only one policy, none of them earns its place yet. Add them when a real second policy arrives.

media.alt: A public library circulation desk with wooden counters, computer screens, a self-service kiosk and a sign reading Return all materials here
media.lead: The desk coordinates; the catalogue knows.
media.caption: At a circulation desk, staff take your request, check the library's records and give you an answer. They do not memorise which copies are on the shelves; the records know that. Counter plays the same part: it turns a borrow request into a call to stock.take() and a reply. The rule about whether a copy is left stays in Stock.

media.alt: A shop wall covered in about a dozen wall clocks for sale, round, square and octagonal, every one showing a different time
media.lead: Copies of the same knowledge drift apart.
media.caption: Every clock on this wall is meant to tell the same time, and no two of them agree. Copies drift. A rule written in two places, such as a pass mark, is a pair of clocks: change one, forget the other, and the program contradicts itself. DRY means one source for each piece of knowledge, like one passes function that every caller asks. Where it breaks: two pieces of code that merely look alike are not always the same rule; merge them only when they share a meaning.

media.title: The General Problem
media.alt: xkcd comic in three panels. A person at a dinner table asks: Can you pass the salt? In the last panel they complain: I said... it's been 20 minutes! The other person replies: I know! I'm developing a system to pass you arbitrary condiments. It'll save time in the long run!
media.caption: YAGNI: build what this program needs now. A general condiment-passing system for one salt shaker is a design with no customer.

media.alt: A replica of the international prototype kilogram: a small polished metal cylinder under two nested glass bell jars on a metal base
media.text: For more than a century, the kilogram was defined by one object: a small polished cylinder of platinum-iridium, the International Prototype of the Kilogram. National standards were calibrated against it or its copies, and the measured mass of each standard drifted a little over time. In November 2018 the world's measurement community voted to define the kilogram by the Planck constant, a fixed constant of nature, instead. One authoritative source, not a pile of copies: DRY on a planetary scale. Sources:

questions.q: What is a sound interpretation of single responsibility?
questions.correct: A class groups behaviour around one coherent responsibility.
wrong: A class must contain exactly one method, including its constructors and getters.
A class must combine every application feature so all changes occur in one file.
A class must have no fields, because storing data always creates a second responsibility.
questions.why: The responsibility is a cohesive concept and reason for change, not a method count.

questions.q: What does dependency inversion encourage in the pricing example?
questions.correct: Make Basket depend on the pricing capability it needs.
wrong: Make every PriceRule depend on the concrete internal fields of Basket in both directions.
Make Basket construct one fixed StudentPrice internally so callers cannot choose another.
Make all fields public so the classes can change one another without method calls.
questions.why: The high-level caller asks for a contract and receives a suitable implementation.

questions.q: Which change most clearly breaks substitutability for List.add(value)?
questions.correct: Making it insert at the front instead of appending at the end.
wrong: Replacing a backing array with linked nodes while preserving all promised list behaviour.
Using a larger internal capacity while preserving element order and all public operations.
Changing a private helper name while preserving the same public contract and outputs.
questions.why: Callers depend on the append contract, not the private storage arrangement.

questions.q: When does YAGNI advise against adding a new feature?
questions.correct: When it exists only for an imagined future need.
wrong: When the current requirements already require it and a user cannot complete the task without it.
When an existing concrete bug needs a fix to preserve the documented input contract.
When an existing test shows the current implementation returns the wrong result.
questions.why: The principle cautions against speculation; required behaviour and bug fixes still matter.

misc.title: SOLID and GRASP at a glance
misc.html:
Reference, not reading. Use each principle as a question about real code.

SOLID

PrincipleQuestion to askWarning signThis week
SSingle responsibilityHow many reasons to change does this class have?pricing, wording and saving in one classOrder and format_receipt
OOpen–closedCan I add a case without editing working code?an if-chain that grows with every new casenew PriceRule classes
LLiskov substitutionDoes the replacement keep every promise?a subclass that throws, ignores or reordersArrayList vs LinkedList; the square
IInterface segregationDoes this caller use everything it is given?a parameter with many methods, only one usednotify needs only send
DDependency inversionDoes the policy create a detail it could be given instead?new of a concrete collaborator inside a classBasket(PriceRule)

GRASP: nine patterns

PatternQuestion it answersThis week
Information ExpertWho has the data for this job?Line.subtotal()
CreatorWho should create this object?Order.addLine creates the Line
ControllerWho first receives a request from outside?Counter.borrow()
Low CouplingHow can this class know less about others?order.deliveryCity()
High CohesionDo this class’s parts belong together?formatting kept out of Order
PolymorphismBehaviour varies by type: who picks it?each rule’s own apply
Pure FabricationNo domain class fits: may I invent one?a receipt formatter
IndirectionCan a go-between keep two classes apart?the PriceRule interface
Protected VariationsWhat will change, and what shields the rest?the clock passed to Greeter

misc.title: Where the principles came from
misc.html:
Each principle was someone’s answer to a real problem: programs that were too hard to change.

1972

Hiding the decisions likely to change

David Parnas publishes “On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules” in Communications of the ACM. Hide each decision likely to change inside its own module. Most of this week grows from that idea.

1974

Coupling and cohesion get their names

Wayne Stevens, Glenford Myers and Larry Constantine’s “Structured Design” (IBM Systems Journal) judges a module split by its coupling and cohesion.

1987

Substitution

Barbara Liskov’s OOPSLA keynote Data Abstraction and Hierarchy asks when one type can safely replace another. With Jeannette Wing she makes it precise in 1994. She received the 2009 ACM Turing Award.

1988

Open for extension

Bertrand Meyer’s Object-Oriented Software Construction states the open–closed principle.

1989

CRC cards

Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham present CRC cards at OOPSLA, to teach object-oriented thinking with index cards.

1999

Refactoring, DRY and YAGNI

Martin Fowler’s Refactoring and Hunt and Thomas’s The Pragmatic Programmer (which coins DRY) appear. Extreme Programming spreads YAGNI.

2000

The principles collected

Robert C. Martin’s paper Design Principles and Design Patterns collects the principles later called SOLID. Michael Feathers coins the acronym around 2004.

Liskov’s original wording

If for each object o1 of type S there is an object o2 of type T such that for all programs P defined in terms of T, the behavior of P is unchanged when o1 is substituted for o2 then S is a subtype of T.

Barbara Liskov, Data Abstraction and Hierarchy, SIGPLAN Notices, May 1988

In plain words: if every program written for T behaves the same when handed an S, then S really is a kind of T. That is the square-and-rectangle test.

Read more

SOLID · GRASP · Beck & Cunningham, CRC cards (1989) · Fowler on YAGNI
